system.text:
You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

messages.content:
Parties: we represent Juniper Ridge Health, Inc.; counterparty is Cobalt Cloud Services LLC.

Rule:
ID: TRANSITION
Title: Post-termination transition assistance and data return
Kind: missing
Summary: When it ends, we get our data back and help moving.
Severity: medium
Category: transition
Position — preferred:
On expiry or termination, Vendor provides transition assistance for up to 6 months at then-current rates, returns Customer Data in a standard machine-readable format within 30 days, and certifies deletion thereafter.

Position — fallback:
90 days of transition assistance; data export within 30 days.
Position — walk-away:
No data return, or immediate deletion of Customer Data on termination.
Detection guidance:
Look for transition, exit, data return/export, deletion timing. Absence in a services/hosting agreement is a deviation (insert).
Redline guidance:
Insert a transition-assistance and data-return paragraph in the termination section.
Model language:
Upon expiry or termination of this Agreement for any reason, Vendor shall (a) at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six (6) months at Vendor's then-current rates; (b) within thirty (30) days, return all Customer Data in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (c) thereafter delete Customer Data from its systems and certify such deletion in writing.

input.quote: 2.1 Customer commits to purchase at least USD 2,000,000 of Services in each of the next three years on a take-or-pay basis, without reduction or termination rights.
input.rationale: § 2.1 imposes a multi-year (three-year) USD 2,000,000 per year take-or-pay commitment on us expressly "without reduction or termination rights" — squarely the playbook's walk-away position and well short of the fallback (single 12-month commitment, reducible on 30 days' notice, true-up rather than penalty). It also directly contradicts § 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no minimum-volume commitment, and sits oddly with § 7.1's bar on undisclosed minimum-use charges. Because the deal is structured around committed spend, we narrowed to the fallback with a minimal edit (12-month term only, 30 days' notice reduction/termination, true-up with no penalty) rather than deleting the commitment outright, while offering deletion as the preferred alternative.

proposal.summary: Narrow the three-year take-or-pay to a single 12-month commitment that is reducible on 30 days' notice with a true-up instead of a penalty.
proposal.comment: [Playbook] We cannot accept a three-year take-or-pay with no reduction or termination right, and it contradicts § 12.3's acknowledgement that we have given no minimum-volume commitment. We have narrowed the commitment to the current 12-month term, reducible on 30 days' notice, with a true-up rather than a shortfall penalty; alternatively we are happy to delete § 2.1 and pay for Services used or ordered.

ops.oldText: 2.1 Customer commits to purchase at least USD 2,000,000 of Services in each of the next three years on a take-or-pay basis, without reduction or termination rights.
ops.newText: 2.1 Customer commits to purchase at least USD 2,000,000 of Services during the current twelve-month term only, and no commitment applies to any subsequent term unless the parties agree otherwise in writing. Customer may reduce or terminate the commitment on 30 days' written notice. If Services ordered in the applicable twelve-month term are less than the committed amount, Customer's sole obligation is to pay a true-up equal to the difference between the committed amount (as reduced) and the Fees for Services ordered, and no penalty, liquidated damages, or accelerated Fees apply.

You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Parties: we represent Juniper Ridge Health, Inc.; counterparty is Cobalt Cloud Services LLC.

Rule:
ID: MINCOMMIT
Title: Minimum purchase commitments and volume restrictions on Customer
Kind: presence
Summary: We do not take-or-pay without an exit.
Severity: medium
Category: commercial
Position — preferred:
No minimum commitment; fees are for usage or ordered services only.
Position — fallback:
Commitment limited to the current 12-month term, reducible on 30 days' notice, with a true-up rather than a penalty.
Position — walk-away:
Multi-year take-or-pay commitments with no reduction or termination right.
Detection guidance:
"minimum", "commit to purchase", "take or pay", "shortfall", volume caps on Customer usage. Commitments the Vendor makes to us are fine.
Redline guidance:
Delete or narrow to the fallback with minimal edits; replace shortfall penalties with a true-up.

input.quote: 2.1 Customer commits to purchase at least USD 2,000,000 of Services in each of the next three years on a take-or-pay basis, without reduction or termination rights.
input.rationale: § 2.1 imposes a multi-year (three-year) USD 2,000,000 per year take-or-pay commitment on us expressly "without reduction or termination rights" — squarely the playbook's walk-away position and well short of the fallback (single 12-month commitment, reducible on 30 days' notice, true-up rather than penalty). It also directly contradicts § 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no minimum-volume commitment, and sits oddly with § 7.1's bar on undisclosed minimum-use charges. Because the deal is structured around committed spend, we narrowed to the fallback with a minimal edit (12-month term only, 30 days' notice reduction/termination, true-up with no penalty) rather than deleting the commitment outright, while offering deletion as the preferred alternative.

You are a precise customer-side contract drafter handling one playbook rule.
Use the document tools to inspect only the clauses needed, including definitions and cross-references.
Reason about direction: identify who is bound and do not flag obligations that benefit our party.
Every quote and replace.oldText must be a verbatim substring from a tool response. Quotes must be 600 characters or fewer.
Apply the playbook's classification semantics: a clause that meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms is compliant — do not redline it. When a clause genuinely fails the fallback, make the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position; use fallback language only when the rule guidance or the existing bargain makes preferred disproportionate.
Comments must begin with the supplied playbook prefix, use concise first-person-plural language, and explain the change and reason.
For deviation or missing findings, call propose_redline and obtain ok:true before submit_finding.
For compliant findings, do not propose a redline. Call submit_finding exactly once, then stop calling tools.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Parties: we represent Juniper Ridge Health, Inc.; counterparty is Cobalt Cloud Services LLC.

Rule:
ID: TRANSITION
Title: Post-termination transition assistance and data return
Kind: missing
Summary: When it ends, we get our data back and help moving.
Severity: medium
Category: transition
Position — preferred:
On expiry or termination, Vendor provides transition assistance for up to 6 months at then-current rates, returns Customer Data in a standard machine-readable format within 30 days, and certifies deletion thereafter.

Position — fallback:
90 days of transition assistance; data export within 30 days.
Position — walk-away:
No data return, or immediate deletion of Customer Data on termination.
Detection guidance:
Look for transition, exit, data return/export, deletion timing. Absence in a services/hosting agreement is a deviation (insert).
Redline guidance:
Insert a transition-assistance and data-return paragraph in the termination section.
Model language:
Upon expiry or termination of this Agreement for any reason, Vendor shall (a) at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six (6) months at Vendor's then-current rates; (b) within thirty (30) days, return all Customer Data in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (c) thereafter delete Customer Data from its systems and certify such deletion in writing.

**Finding: deviation (MINCOMMIT)** — § 2.1 (p0012), cross-read against § 12.3 (p0044) and § 7.1 (p0025).

- **Issue:** § 2.1 binds us to a three-year, USD 2,000,000/year take-or-pay "without reduction or termination rights" — the playbook's walk-away position, and inconsistent with § 12.3 where Vendor acknowledges we have given no minimum-volume commitment.
- **Redline (validated, ok:true):** narrowed to the fallback — commitment limited to the current 12-month term, reducible/terminable on 30 days' written notice, and any gap settled by a true-up with no penalty, liquidated damages, or accelerated Fees.
- **Negotiation note:** the comment offers outright deletion of § 2.1 (pay for Services used or ordered) as the preferred alternative, consistent with precedent seed-mincommit.

system.text:
You are an independent verifier of one proposed contract finding.
Judge the proposal against the supplied playbook rule, original paragraphs, resolved definitions, deterministic checks, rendered redline, and comment.
Do not rely on hidden drafter reasoning. Fail invalid, directionally wrong, or rule-incomplete edits.
Deterministic checks are heuristics (regular expressions and a changed-character ratio), not verdicts: a failed regex may simply be a phrasing variant, and a high changed-character ratio is acceptable when the rule genuinely requires rewriting the clause (for example replacing a governing-law sentence or deleting a take-or-pay obligation). Weigh them as evidence and decide on substance: does the redline reach the playbook position with the smallest edit that does so, and is the comment accurate?
The claimed status matters: for a compliant finding, no redline or counterparty comment is expected, and you should pass when the cited text supports compliance. Fail a deviation finding whose cited clause already meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms (the playbook's classification semantics) — a redline that merely upgrades an acceptable fallback to preferred wording is over-flagging. Compliant findings are retained as internal evaluation evidence, not raised as negotiation issues. For deviation or missing findings, require an actionable valid proposal.
Return a concise verdict with actionable reasons.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

Commitment limited to the current 12-month term, reducible on 30 days' notice, with a true-up rather than a penalty.
Position — walk-away:
Multi-year take-or-pay commitments with no reduction or termination right.
Detection guidance:
"minimum", "commit to purchase", "take or pay", "shortfall", volume caps on Customer usage. Commitments the Vendor makes to us are fine.
Redline guidance:
Delete or narrow to the fallback with minimal edits; replace shortfall penalties with a true-up.

Claimed finding status: deviation

Finding rationale:
§ 2.1 imposes a multi-year (three-year) USD 2,000,000 per year take-or-pay commitment on us expressly "without reduction or termination rights" — squarely the playbook's walk-away position and well short of the fallback (single 12-month commitment, reducible on 30 days' notice, true-up rather than penalty). It also directly contradicts § 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no minimum-volume commitment, and sits oddly with § 7.1's bar on undisclosed minimum-use charges. Because the deal is structured around committed spend, we narrowed to the fallback with a minimal edit (12-month term only, 30 days' notice reduction/termination, true-up with no penalty) rather than deleting the commitment outright, while offering deletion as the preferred alternative.

Original paragraphs:

p0012: 2.1 Customer commits to purchase at least USD 2,000,000 of Services during the current twelve-month term only, and no commitment applies to any subsequent term unless the parties agree otherwise in writing. If Services ordered in the applicable twelve-month term are less than the committed amount, Customer's sole obligation is to pay a true-up equal to the difference between the committed amount (as reduced) and the Fees for Services ordered, and no penalty, liquidated damages, or accelerated Fees apply.

input.quote: 10.1 On expiry or termination, Customer's right to access terminated subscription Services ends after any agreed transition period. Rights in accepted Deliverables, paid-up licences, Customer Data, and materials Customer owned or licensed independently continue according to their terms.
input.rationale: Section 10 (Effect of Expiry or Termination) contains no exit-assistance or data-return obligation. Section 10.1 merely presupposes "any agreed transition period" without obliging Vendor to provide one, and 10.2 covers only Deliverables and refunds. Searches for transition, export, return and deletion language return nothing else: Section 15 (Customer Data and Privacy) addresses processing limits only, and Section 16.5 excludes Customer Data from the return-or-destroy duty by referring it to "Sections 11 and 15" — but no Section 11 exists in the document. As a hosted-services agreement with no data return or export right, this fails the fallback (90 days' assistance plus export within 30 days), so we insert a new Section 10.3 at the preferred position: up to six months' transition assistance at then-current rates, return of Customer Data in a machine-readable format within 30 days, and certified deletion thereafter (with a carve-out for routine backups and legal retention, consistent with Section 16.5).

How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.

No data return, or immediate deletion of Customer Data on termination.

content.text:
**Finding: missing (medium severity) — transition assistance and data return.**

The Agreement has no exit clause. Section 10.1 assumes "any agreed transition period" without obliging Vendor to provide one; Section 10.2 covers only Deliverables and refunds. There is no data return, export, or deletion obligation anywhere — Section 15 governs processing only, and Section 16.5 carves Customer Data out of the return-or-destroy duty by deferring to "Sections 11 and 15," yet **Section 11 does not exist in the document** (the outline runs 10.2 → 12). So the carve-out points nowhere, leaving us with no contractual right to get our data back.

That fails even the fallback (90 days' assistance plus 30-day export), so I inserted a new Section 10.3 at the preferred position: up to six months' transition assistance at Vendor's then-current rates, return of Customer Data in a machine-readable format within 30 days, and certified deletion thereafter — with a backups/legal-retention carve-out for consistency with Section 16.5. The comment offers 90 days as a fallback. Redline validated (ok:true) against the seed-transition precedent.

You are an independent verifier of one proposed contract finding.
Judge the proposal against the supplied playbook rule, original paragraphs, resolved definitions, deterministic checks, rendered redline, and comment.
Do not rely on hidden drafter reasoning. Fail invalid, directionally wrong, or rule-incomplete edits.
Deterministic checks are heuristics (regular expressions and a changed-character ratio), not verdicts: a failed regex may simply be a phrasing variant, and a high changed-character ratio is acceptable when the rule genuinely requires rewriting the clause (for example replacing a governing-law sentence or deleting a take-or-pay obligation). Weigh them as evidence and decide on substance: does the redline reach the playbook position with the smallest edit that does so, and is the comment accurate?
The claimed status matters: for a compliant finding, no redline or counterparty comment is expected, and you should pass when the cited text supports compliance. Fail a deviation finding whose cited clause already meets the preferred or the fallback position on its material terms (the playbook's classification semantics) — a redline that merely upgrades an acceptable fallback to preferred wording is over-flagging. Compliant findings are retained as internal evaluation evidence, not raised as negotiation issues. For deviation or missing findings, require an actionable valid proposal.
Return a concise verdict with actionable reasons.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

You are in-house counsel producing a concise Markdown issues memo from verified findings.
Include: Executive summary; a Markdown table of findings with severity, rule, status and section; Walk-away items; Next steps.
Never invent a section reference or legal conclusion. Use only supplied findings.

We represent the customer.
Our party aliases: Customer, Client, Licensee, Company, Buyer, Purchaser, Subscriber, User.
Counterparty aliases: Vendor, Supplier, Provider, Service Provider, Licensor, Contractor, Consultant, Seller, Host.
Comment prefix: [Playbook].
Tone: Concise, professional, first person plural ("we"). Explain what changed and why in one or two sentences, cite the playbook position, offer the fallback where sensible, never lecture.


How to classify a clause against a rule (this is how the reviewing team reads its own playbook):
- compliant: the clause meets the preferred position, OR it meets the fallback position on its material terms. A clause at the fallback is acceptable and is not redlined; say in the rationale that it sits at the fallback.
- deviation: the clause fails the fallback on a material term, or falls into walk-away territory. Only then propose a redline.
- missing: the rule expects a clause and no usable clause exists anywhere in the document.
- Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording (a missing reminder mechanic, a missing price-uplift cap, 'paid' versus 'paid or payable', an accepted-but-not-preferred governing law) are noted in the rationale, not flagged as deviations.
- Do not flag a clause that benefits our party. Do not flag the same commercial term twice under two rules unless both rules are independently breached.

{"markdown":"# Issues Memo — Master Services Agreement

**To:** Deal team  
**From:** Legal (Customer-side review)  
**Re:** Playbook review of the Master Services Agreement — verified findings

---

## 1. Executive summary

We reviewed the Master Services Agreement against our playbook and verified 19 findings. Nine clauses meet our positions and require no redline: limitation of liability (§ 21), assignment and change of control (§ 24), liquidated damages (none imposed on us), audit rights (§ 22), auto-renewal (§ 8.2–8.3), performance warranty (§ 19), and Vendor insurance (§ 18). Several of these — the mutual cap with full carve-outs, the renewal reminder mechanic and uplift cap, and the Vendor insurance programme — run affirmatively in our favour.

The remaining ten findings are deviations or gaps, and the concentration of risk is unusual. Three items are missing entirely: there is no indemnification article anywhere in the Agreement (the outline jumps from § 19 to § 21, leaving orphaned cross-references in §§ 9.3, 19.4, 21.3 and 30.5), no Customer termination-for-convenience right across a three-year term, and no post-termination transition assistance or data-return obligation. We also note an internal drafting problem the Vendor should own: §§ 2.1, 7.2, 12.4 and 28.1 each contradict acknowledgements or provisions the Vendor itself has given (§ 12.3 confirms we made no exclusivity, MFN, minimum-volume or no-hire commitment; § 28.2 confers exclusive New York jurisdiction). No redline. |

---

## 3. Walk-away items

The following findings sit in walk-away territory under the playbook and should be treated as conditions of signature rather than negotiating preferences:

1. **No Vendor indemnity (new § 20 required).** The complete absence of a Vendor IP-infringement indemnity is walk-away, and the Agreement's own cross-references assume one exists.
2. **§ 14.2 — Deliverable licence.** Revocable at Vendor's discretion, term-limited, and excluding Affiliates and contractors.
3. **§ 12.4 — Non-compete.** Post-term restriction beyond 12 months, undefined scope, no territory limit, and no internal-development or acquisition carve-out.
4. **§ 12.4 — No-hire.** 24-month post-term no-hire covering all Vendor employees with carve-outs expressly negated.
5. **No Customer termination for convenience.** Absence of any convenience right in a term longer than 12 months.
6. **§ 7.2 — Disclose-and-match / MFN.** Open-ended exclusivity and MFN obligations imposed on us.
7. **§ 2.1 — Take-or-pay.** Three-year commitment expressly without reduction or termination rights.
8. **§ 28.1 — Singapore law and exclusive Singapore jurisdiction.**

We would also treat the § 14.2 ownership position (IP rule) as effectively non-negotiable in its current form, since it fails both the preferred and fallback positions for work product we commission and pay for under § 1.4.

---

## 4. Next steps

1. **Issue the redline** covering the ten deviation and missing findings: new § 20 (Indemnification), new § 10.3 (Transition and data return), a new Customer convenience-termination right with a conforming edit to § 2.1, reversal of § 14.2 ownership and licence terms, deletion of § 12.4's non-compete, narrowing of § 12.4's no-hire, deletion of § 7.2 (first instance), narrowing of § 2.1's take-or-pay to the fallback, and substitution of New York law in § 28.1.
2. **Flag the internal inconsistencies to Vendor** as drafting defects it should resolve in its own interest: the § 12.3 acknowledgement contradicting §§ 2.1, 7.2 and 12.4; the § 28.1/§ 28.2 jurisdiction conflict; the duplicate clause numbering at 7.2; the orphaned § 20.5 cross-reference in § 9.3; and the reference in § 16.5 to a non-existent Section 11.
3. **Confirm the commercial mandate on § 2.1** before the first call. We have proposed the fallback (single 12-month commitment, reducible on 30 days' notice, true-up rather than penalty) rather than deletion, on the assumption that committed spend is central to the pricing. Please confirm whether deletion is the preferred ask.
4. **Hold the compliant clauses.** Sections 8, 18, 19, 21, 22 and 24 should be preserved as drafted; we will resist any Vendor attempt to reopen them in exchange for movement elsewhere, particularly the § 21.3 carve-outs, which the new indemnity article relies on.
5. **Escalate if Vendor refuses** on any walk-away item, and in particular on the indemnity and convenience-termination gaps, which cannot be cured by commercial concession."}
